lec05kp06-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp06-u01-p1-title.text: The step function has no slope to read, so we cannot tell which way to move a weight

lec05kp06-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp06-u01-p1-bridge.text: KP05 grew the network step by step and the rules gave the weights directly. To let the network learn its weights, we must know which way to move them. Can the step function do that?

lec05kp06-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp06-step-slope
lec05kp06-u01-p1-fig1.text: Top: the step function has slope 0 apart from the jump at 0 and no slope at the jump. Bottom: the sigmoid with a tangent of slope 0.25 in the middle.

image.alt: Top: the step function has slope 0 apart from the jump at 0 and no slope at the jump. Bottom: the sigmoid with a tangent of slope 0.25 in the middle.

lec05kp06-u01-p1-term:代價函數.name: term:Cost function
lec05kp06-u01-p1-term:代價函數.text: **Cost function**: one number that adds up how far the predictions are from the targets; smaller is better. From here on the example uses $E=\tfrac12(\text{target}-\text{output})^2$.

lec05kp06-u01-p1-term:梯度下降.name: term:Gradient descent
lec05kp06-u01-p1-term:梯度下降.text: **Gradient descent**: read the slope of the cost in every weight and move the weight a little in the direction that lowers the cost.

lec05kp06-u01-p1-c.name: u01-p1-c
lec05kp06-u01-p1-c.text: **The problem with a step**: apart from the jump the step function has slope 0, and at the jump it has no slope. Without a slope, gradient descent has nothing to work with.

lec05kp06-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp06-u01-p2-title.text: A sigmoid gives a slope everywhere, but nearer to a step the slope is narrower

lec05kp06-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp06-u01-p2-bridge.text: The step function has no usable slope. If we replace it by a smooth curve with a slope everywhere, what does that slope look like?

lec05kp06-u01-p2-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp06-sigmoid-a
lec05kp06-u01-p2-fig1.text: Top: three sigmoids (a=0.7, 2, 8) with the dashed step, a larger a is closer to the step. Bottom: their slopes, a taller and narrower spike for a larger a with almost zero tails.

image.alt: Top: three sigmoids (a=0.7, 2, 8) with the dashed step, a larger a is closer to the step. Bottom: their slopes, a taller and narrower spike for a larger a with almost zero tails.

lec05kp06-u01-p2-term:sigmoid.name: term:Sigmoid
lec05kp06-u01-p2-term:sigmoid.text: **Sigmoid**: $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-ax}}$ squeezes any number into 0 to 1, and a larger $a$ is closer to the step. Its slope is $f'(x)=a\,f(x)\,(1-f(x))$.

lec05kp06-u01-p2-c1.name: u01-p2-c1
lec05kp06-u01-p2-c1.text: **The closer to a step, the harder to train**: a larger $a$ makes the slope a taller, narrower spike with almost zero slope on both sides (bottom plot).

lec05kp06-u01-p2-c2.name: u01-p2-c2
lec05kp06-u01-p2-c2.text: **A trade-off**: once we leave the step the output is no longer just 0 or 1, the earlier picture of cube corners no longer holds and the cost function carries the classification. Later examples use $a=1$.

lec05kp06-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp06-u01-p3-title.text: Walk a small 2-2-1 network through: input (1,0), target 1, output 0.471

lec05kp06-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp06-u01-p3-bridge.text: The sigmoid gave a slope everywhere. Walk a small 2-2-1 network (2 inputs, 2 hidden units, 1 output) through: with input $(1,0)$, what is the output?

lec05kp06-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp06-net-forward
lec05kp06-u01-p3-fig1.text: Forward pass of the 2-2-1 network: input (1,0); hidden unit 1 has sum 0.10 and output 0.525; unit 2 has sum −0.20 and output 0.450; the output unit has sum −0.118 and output 0.471 with target 1; weights are written beside the lines.

image.alt: Forward pass of the 2-2-1 network: input (1,0); hidden unit 1 has sum 0.10 and output 0.525; unit 2 has sum −0.20 and output 0.450; the output unit has sum −0.118 and output 0.471 with target 1; weights are written beside the lines.

lec05kp06-u01-p3-term:前向傳遞.name: term:Forward pass
lec05kp06-u01-p3-term:前向傳遞.text: **Forward pass**: compute layer by layer from the input. Each unit first forms the weighted sum $v$ and then applies the sigmoid to get $y=f(v)$, and the intermediate values are stored.

lec05kp06-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp06-u01-p4-title.text: How much to change one weight: split the cost's slope into three slopes multiplied together

lec05kp06-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp06-u01-p4-bridge.text: The output 0.471 is still 0.529 from the target. Take one output-layer weight, from hidden unit 1 to the output: how do we compute the slope of the cost $E$ in it?

lec05kp06-u01-p4-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp06-chain
lec05kp06-u01-p4-fig1.text: Chain rule: the slope from w to v is the input 0.525, from v to o is 0.249 and from o to E is −0.529; their product is −0.069.

image.alt: Chain rule: the slope from w to v is the input 0.525, from v to o is 0.249 and from o to E is −0.529; their product is −0.069.

lec05kp06-u01-p4-term:連鎖律.name: term:Chain rule
lec05kp06-u01-p4-term:連鎖律.text: **Chain rule**: $E$ depends on the weight $w$ only through $o$ and $v$, so the slope is a product of three: $\dfrac{\partial E}{\partial w}=\dfrac{\partial E}{\partial o}\cdot\dfrac{\partial o}{\partial v}\cdot\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial w}$.

lec05kp06-u01-p4-c1.name: u01-p4-c1
lec05kp06-u01-p4-c1.text: **The three slopes**: $\partial E/\partial o=-e=-0.529$; $\partial o/\partial v=f'(v_o)=o(1-o)=0.249$; $\partial v/\partial w=y_1=0.525$ (the input this weight multiplies; a bias has input 1).

lec05kp06-u01-p4-c2.name: u01-p4-c2
lec05kp06-u01-p4-c2.text: **Multiply**: $-0.529\times0.249\times0.525=-0.069$. The minus sign means that increasing $w$ lowers $E$.

lec05kp06-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp06-u01-p5-title.text: Merge the first two factors into the error signal δ: the downhill step is δ times the input

lec05kp06-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp06-u01-p5-bridge.text: A weight's slope is the product of three slopes, two of which concern only the output unit. Can we merge them into one quantity for all three output weights?

lec05kp06-u01-p5-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp06-out-bars
lec05kp06-u01-p5-fig1.text: Updates of the three output-layer weights (η=0.3, δ_o=0.1319): bias +0.0396, from hidden unit 1 +0.0208, from unit 2 +0.0178.

image.alt: Updates of the three output-layer weights (η=0.3, δ_o=0.1319): bias +0.0396, from hidden unit 1 +0.0208, from unit 2 +0.0178.

lec05kp06-u01-p5-term:誤差訊號.name: term:Error signal
lec05kp06-u01-p5-term:誤差訊號.text: **Error signal $\delta$**: $\delta=-\partial E/\partial v$, that is, 'error times slope'. Output unit: $\delta_o=e\,f'(v_o)=0.529\times0.249=0.1319$.

lec05kp06-u01-p5-term:學習率.name: term:Learning rate
lec05kp06-u01-p5-term:學習率.text: **Learning rate $\eta$**: the step size of each weight update. Here $\eta=0.3$.

lec05kp06-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp06-u01-p5-c1.text: **Descent direction = $\delta$ × input**: $-\partial E/\partial w=\delta\cdot$input. For example the slope $-0.069$ on page 4 with its sign flipped is $0.1319\times0.525$.

lec05kp06-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp06-u01-p6-title.text: Hidden units do not see the target: pass the output δ back along the weights

lec05kp06-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp06-u01-p6-bridge.text: The error signal gives the output-layer weights their downhill step, $\delta_o$ times the input. Hidden units do not see the target directly, so where do their $\delta$ come from?

lec05kp06-u01-p6-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp06-net-backward
lec05kp06-u01-p6-fig1.text: Backpropagation: red lines show the error travelling back from the output, δ_o=0.1319, hidden unit 1 δ=0.0164, unit 2 δ=−0.0131.

image.alt: Backpropagation: red lines show the error travelling back from the output, δ_o=0.1319, hidden unit 1 δ=0.0164, unit 2 δ=−0.0131.

lec05kp06-u01-p6-term:反向傳播.name: term:Backpropagation
lec05kp06-u01-p6-term:反向傳播.text: **Backpropagation**: after the forward pass, go backward from the output layer. A unit's $\delta$ is the sum of the next layer's $\delta$ times the connecting weights, times the unit's own slope.

lec05kp06-u01-p6-c1.name: u01-p6-c1
lec05kp06-u01-p6-c1.text: **Why back**: a hidden unit affects $E$ only through the next layer's weights: $\delta_j=f'(v_j)\sum_k\delta_k\,w_{kj}$.

lec05kp06-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp06-u01-p7-title.text: After one step on all nine weights the output moves from 0.471 toward 1 and the cost drops from 0.140 to 0.132

lec05kp06-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp06-u01-p7-bridge.text: All nine weights now have their $\delta$. If every weight moves by $\eta\times\delta\times$input, does the output really get closer to the target?

lec05kp06-u01-p7-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp06-before-after
lec05kp06-u01-p7-fig1.text: Before and after one update: the output o goes from 0.4706 to 0.4857 (target 1) and the cost E drops from 0.1401 to 0.1322.

image.alt: Before and after one update: the output o goes from 0.4706 to 0.4857 (target 1) and the cost E drops from 0.1401 to 0.1322.

lec05kp06-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp06-u01-p7-c1.text: **Hidden-layer update**: the inputs are $(1,1,0)$. Unit 1's bias and $x_1$ weight each get $+0.0049$; unit 2's each get $-0.0039$; the $x_2$ weights stay (the input is 0).

lec05kp06-u01-p7-c3.name: u01-p7-c3
lec05kp06-u01-p7-c3.text: **One step is small**: $E$ drops only a little, so many repeats are needed to approach the target.

lec05kp06-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp06-u01-p8-title.text: Check with numerical slopes: δ×input of all nine weights agrees with the difference quotient

lec05kp06-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp06-u01-p8-bridge.text: After one step the cost drops from 0.140 to 0.132, but one good step does not prove that every $\delta$ is right. Is there a way to verify the nine slopes without the derivation?

lec05kp06-u01-p8-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp06-numcheck
lec05kp06-u01-p8-fig1.text: The slopes of the nine weights from δ×input (bars) coincide with the numerical difference slopes (dots).

image.alt: The slopes of the nine weights from δ×input (bars) coincide with the numerical difference slopes (dots).

lec05kp06-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp06-u01-p8-c1.text: **Numerical check**: shift one weight by a tiny $\varepsilon=10^{-6}$ up and down and see how much $E$ changes: $[E(w+\varepsilon)-E(w-\varepsilon)]/(2\varepsilon)$.

lec05kp06-u01-p8-c2.name: u01-p8-c2
lec05kp06-u01-p8-c2.text: **Result**: for all nine weights $-\delta\times$input equals the difference slope, within $10^{-6}$ (bars are from $\delta$, dots from the difference).

lec05kp06-u01-p8-c3.name: u01-p8-c3
lec05kp06-u01-p8-c3.text: **Next**: how is the whole procedure written as an algorithm, and what must we watch in practice? (the next KP)

lec05kp06-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp06-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: a larger a is closer to a step, yet the slope at distance 3 is almost 0

lec05kp06-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp06-u01-p9-bridge.text: The numerical check passed: $\delta\times$input agrees with the difference slopes. Back to the sigmoid's slope parameter $a$: if we make it larger to be closer to a step, what does that do to training?

lec05kp06-u01-p9-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp06-saturation
lec05kp06-u01-p9-fig1.text: Logarithmic bar chart of the sigmoid slope at x=3: 0.068 for a=0.7, 0.0049 for a=2 and 3×10⁻¹⁰ for a=8.

image.alt: Logarithmic bar chart of the sigmoid slope at x=3: 0.068 for a=0.7, 0.0049 for a=2 and 3×10⁻¹⁰ for a=8.

lec05kp06-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp06-u01-p9-c2.text: **Meaning**: with a large $a$ the sigmoid saturates not far from the centre, $\delta$ is multiplied by a slope near 0 and the weights hardly move.

lec05kp06-u01-p9-c3.name: u01-p9-c3
lec05kp06-u01-p9-c3.text: **Trade-off**: the closer to a step, the harder to train by gradients, so $a$ is chosen moderate.

lec05kp06-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp06-u01-p10-title.text: Extension: practice, change the target to 0: which way do the output-layer δ and weights move?

lec05kp06-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp06-u01-p10-bridge.text: Saturation makes the slope almost 0 and $\delta$ small. Back in the example (slope 0.249), change only the target from 1 to 0: how do the sign of the output-layer $\delta$ and the update direction change?

lec05kp06-u01-p10-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp06-practice-net
lec05kp06-u01-p10-fig1.text: Practice figure: the same 2-2-1 network and forward numbers with the target changed to 0.

image.alt: Practice figure: the same 2-2-1 network and forward numbers with the target changed to 0.

lec05kp06-u01-p10-q1.name: u01-p10-q1
lec05kp06-u01-p10-q1.text: **Question 1**: with target 0, what are the error $e$ and $\delta_o$?

lec05kp06-u01-p10-q2.name: u01-p10-q2
lec05kp06-u01-p10-q2.text: **Question 2**: in which direction does each of the three output weights move, and by how much ($\eta=0.3$)?

lec05kp06-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp06-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2

lec05kp06-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp06-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice changed the target to 0 and asked for $\delta_o$ and the three output updates. Worked out in full, what are the answers?

lec05kp06-u01-p11-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp06-practice-sol
lec05kp06-u01-p11-fig1.text: Output-layer updates for target 0: bias −0.0352, from unit 1 −0.0185, from unit 2 −0.0158, all downward.

image.alt: Output-layer updates for target 0: bias −0.0352, from unit 1 −0.0185, from unit 2 −0.0158, all downward.

lec05kp06-u01-p11-a2.name: u01-p11-a2
lec05kp06-u01-p11-a2.text: **Question 2**: $\Delta w=0.3\times(-0.1173)\times$input: bias $-0.0352$, $w_{o1}$ $-0.0185$, $w_{o2}$ $-0.0158$; all three move down.

lec05kp06-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp06-u01-p11-a3.text: **Check**: the output 0.471 must drop toward 0, so the output weights should decrease; the signs are exactly opposite to the target-1 case.

steps.label: Toward backprop
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Made under CLARITY.md C12 to C18: plain words before terms, titles that state the point, pages linked by questions, a figure on every page. One 2-2-1 network (input (1,0), target 1) with real numbers is used throughout; the numbers were checked by a program and by numerical differences. These notes are public with the file and contain no student IDs, grades or exam questions.

steps.label: Step has no slope
steps.speakerNotes: KP05 grew the network by rules and the rules gave the weights directly. This page asks what we need when the network must learn its weights. The answer is to read the slope of the cost function in each weight and move the weight in the direction that lowers the cost, which is gradient descent. The cost function simply adds up how far predictions are from targets; here it is one half of the squared difference between target and output. The trouble is the step function: in the top plot, apart from the jump the slope is 0, and at the jump there is no slope at all, so no usable slope exists. The bottom plot is the smooth sigmoid with a tangent of slope 0.25 in the middle. The next page looks at what the slope looks like after replacing the step by a sigmoid.

steps.label: Round it: sigmoid
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the step function has no usable slope. This page rounds the step into a sigmoid: it squeezes any number into 0 to 1, a is the slope parameter, a larger a is closer to the step, and the slope is a times f times (1 minus f). The top plot shows three sigmoids with a equal to 0.7, 2 and 8, the dashed line is the step, and the bottom plot shows their slopes. Note the counter-intuitive part: a larger a is closer to a step but its slope becomes a tall, narrow spike with almost zero slope on both sides, so the closer to a step the harder it is to train by gradients. Also, once we leave the step, KP03's picture of mapping to cube corners no longer holds and the cost function carries the classification. The next page walks a small network through.

steps.label: Walk a 2-2-1 net
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page made the slope usable everywhere with the sigmoid. This page walks a small 2-2-1 network through: two inputs, two hidden units and one output, with input 1 and 0 and target 1. The forward pass computes layer by layer, each unit first forming the weighted sum v and then applying the sigmoid, and the intermediate values are stored because we need them later. Hidden unit 1 has weighted sum 0.10 and output 0.525; unit 2 has minus 0.20 and output 0.450. The output unit has weighted sum minus 0.118 and output 0.471, still 0.529 away from the target 1, with cost E equal to 0.140. The weights sit beside the lines in the figure and the biases are written above it. The next page asks how this error of 0.529 is shared among the weights.

steps.label: Chain rule
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page computed the output 0.471 and the error 0.529. This page asks how much one output-layer weight should change, taking the weight from hidden unit 1 to the output. The cost E depends on this weight only through the output o and the weighted sum v, which is the chain rule: the slope of E in the weight is the product of three slopes. The first is the negative error, minus 0.529; the second is the sigmoid slope, o times 1 minus o, which is 0.249; the third is the input this weight multiplies, the output 0.525 of hidden unit 1. Multiplying gives minus 0.069, and the minus sign means that increasing the weight lowers the cost. The next page merges the first two factors into one quantity that serves all three output weights.

steps.label: Error signal
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that one weight's slope is a product of three factors. This page merges the first two, the error and the sigmoid slope, into one quantity called the error signal delta, defined as the negative slope of the cost in the weighted sum; for the output unit it is the error times the slope, 0.529 times 0.249 equals 0.1319. The gradient of each output weight is then delta times that weight's input. The learning rate is the step size of each update, here 0.3. The inputs of the three output weights are 1, 0.525 and 0.450, and the updates are 0.0396, 0.0208 and 0.0178; the three bars point positive, so all three output weights should increase. Delta is the negative slope here, hence the update is added; the source writes delta both as the slope and as error times slope, which differ by a sign, so this deck fixes one definition. The next page asks where the hidden units get their delta, since they do not see the target.

steps.label: Backpropagation
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page gave the output-layer weights their delta. This page asks where hidden units get theirs, since they do not see the target. Backpropagation goes backward from the output layer after the forward pass is done: a unit's delta is the sum of the next layer's deltas times the connecting weights, times the unit's own slope. In this example hidden unit 1 connects to the output with weight 0.50, so delta 1 is 0.249 times 0.1319 times 0.50, which is 0.0164; unit 2 connects with minus 0.40, so delta 2 is minus 0.0131, with the opposite sign, meaning unit 2 should move the other way. The red lines in the figure are the path the error takes backward, using the same weights as the forward pass. The next page updates all nine weights by one step.

steps.label: Cost goes down
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page computed the delta of every hidden unit. This page moves all nine weights by one step of step size times delta times input: the hidden-layer inputs are 1, 1 and 0, so unit 1's bias and x1 weight each increase by 0.0049, unit 2's each decrease by 0.0039, and the x2 weights stay because their input is 0. After recomputing the forward pass the output goes from 0.4706 to 0.4857, a bit closer to the target 1, and the cost drops from 0.1401 to 0.1322. The figure shows the output on the left and the cost on the right. One step is small, and many repeats are needed to approach the target. The next page asks how to confirm that these deltas are right.

steps.label: How to check
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page saw the cost drop after one step, but one good step does not prove that every delta is right. This page checks numerically: shift one weight by a very small number and see how much the cost changes, giving the slope by a difference. In the figure the bars are the slopes computed as delta times input and the dots are the difference slopes; they agree for all nine weights within one millionth. This is the most common debugging method when writing backpropagation code. The numbers on this page are computed for this example, not taken from the source's experiment. What is left open: how the whole procedure is written as an algorithm and what to watch in practice, which is the next KP. The main line ends here and the extension follows.

steps.label: Extension: saturation
steps.speakerNotes: The numerical check on the previous page passed. This page returns to the sigmoid's slope parameter a: what does a larger a, closer to a step, do to training? At x equal to 3 the slope is a times f times 1 minus f: 0.068 for a equal to 0.7, 0.0049 for a equal to 2, and only 3 times 10 to the minus 10 for a equal to 8. The figure uses a logarithmic axis. So with a large a the sigmoid saturates not far from the centre, delta is multiplied by a slope near 0 and the weights hardly move; the closer to a step the harder to train by gradients, and a is chosen moderate. This page is an extension and is not timed. The next page is a practice.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said that saturation makes delta small. This page asks the students to return to the example and change only the target from 1 to 0; the forward numbers stay the same and the figure shows the same network with target 0. Question 1: what are the error and the output-layer delta? The hint is that the error is target minus output and the slope 0.249 stays. Question 2: in which direction does each of the three output weights move and by how much with step size 0.3. The next page gives the complete solution.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed questions 1 and 2 and this page is the complete solution. Question 1: the target is 0 and the output is 0.471, so the error is minus 0.471 and the output-layer delta is minus 0.471 times 0.249, which is minus 0.1173. Question 2: the update is step size 0.3 times delta times input: minus 0.0352 for the bias, minus 0.0185 from hidden unit 1 and minus 0.0158 from unit 2, so all three move down. That makes sense: the output 0.471 must drop toward 0, so the output weights should decrease, with signs exactly opposite to the target-1 case. The three bars in the figure point negative. KP06 ends here and the next KP writes the whole procedure as the backpropagation algorithm.

metadata.title: Pattern Recognition, Chapter 4, KP06: from the step to the gradient of backpropagation (undergraduate, self-study)
